strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: RL training instability in CXR report generation due to fixed KL regularization and static reference policies. The two proposed mechanisms (RER for response-level KL weighting, VAPR for validation-anchored resets) are clearly formulated, and Eq. (3)-(9) plus Algorithm 1 make the method fully reproducible.

Experimental evidence is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against many recent baselines on both MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, ablations isolating each pipeline stage (Tab. 3) and each RL modification (Tab. 4), training-dynamics plots showing where collapse occurs without VAPR (Fig. 3c-d), group-size and model-size sensitivity studies, and a fair resource-comparison table (Tab. S9) documenting the extra supervision prior methods rely on.

The supplementary analysis of reward choice is a genuine strength: the demonstration of reward inversion for RadGraph F1 (Fig. S6) and high group-variance for CheXpert F1, together with the sign-consistency analysis (Eq. 11-12) justifying BLEU-4 as a surrogate for clinical efficacy, is an honest and useful empirical contribution beyond the main method.

Computational overhead of RER is quantified (+1.9% step time, +3.9% memory), and hyperparameters, prompts, and training subsets are disclosed, supporting reproducibility; code is stated to be released.

The three-stage pipeline and classifier-guided prompting show clear ablation-backed gains (recall +22.1% from classifier cues), and qualitative cases illustrate concrete error corrections (localization, hallucination removal).
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. RER is a bounded piecewise-linear heuristic mapping (advantage, normalized reference entropy) to βi, and VAPR is essentially periodic rollback of both policies to the best validation checkpoint. Neither is supported by theoretical analysis (e.g., effect on optimization stability or convergence); the paper would benefit from at least a comparison against simpler alternatives such as re-anchoring to the initial SFT checkpoint rather than the validation-best one, to isolate why validation anchoring specifically matters.

The claimed 'state-of-the-art' is confounded by the base model: REVA-PO uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a much stronger pretrained LVLM than the Llama-2-7B/TinyLlama/GPT-2 backbones of most baselines. While Tab. S9 partially addresses resource fairness, there is no controlled experiment comparing REVA-PO's RL mechanisms on the same backbone as a strong baseline (e.g., GRPO with fixed KL on Qwen2.5-VL-7B under identical pipeline), so the attribution of gains to RER+VAPR versus the stronger initialization is not fully clean (Tab. 4 helps but is limited to MIMIC-CXR).

Results are reported without statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, and several margins are small (e.g., BLEU-4 0.136→0.143 on MIMIC-CXR; METEOR on IU-Xray is below AM-MRG). Single-run comparisons at this granularity are fragile.

Hyperparameter sensitivity for the new mechanisms is not studied in the main paper: no ablation over (βmin, βbase, βmax), the reset period M, or λ in the validation score. Given that RER and VAPR introduce several new knobs, this is a notable gap. IU-Xray CE metrics (CheXpert/RadGraph F1) are also absent, so clinical-accuracy claims rest mainly on MIMIC-CXR.

Optimizing BLEU-4 against a single reference report risks style-imitation reward hacking that inflates overlap metrics; the sign-consistency analysis is post-hoc and evaluated on the same policy being optimized. No human/radiologist evaluation is provided, and there is no limitations or societal-impact discussion for a clinical-facing system.

The RL stage is trained on a 10k random subset of MIMIC-CXR while validation/test are unchanged; the paper should clarify how this interacts with comparisons to baselines trained on the full set, and whether the discard-<30-token filtering biases toward longer reports.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a coherent motivation connecting fixed KL regularization, reference-policy staleness, and training instability in RL for report generation.
RER and VAPR are lightweight, drop-in mechanisms with no auxiliary critic or preference data; the supplementary material quantifies their overhead honestly (+1.9% step time, +3.9% memory).

The ablation studies are thorough: each stage and each RL modification is isolated (Tables 3-4), and stability analyses (Fig. 3) directly visualize collapse behavior with and without the proposed mechanisms.

The supplementary analysis of reward selection (Appendix A) is unusually careful: it documents CheXpert F1's reward variance and RadGraph F1's reward inversion, and provides quantitative sign/Top-1 consistency analysis justifying BLEU-4 as a proxy reward.

Resource comparability is addressed via Table S9, showing most baselines use extra supervision (external corpora, bounding boxes, knowledge graphs), while the proposed method uses only image-level labels.
Additional robustness checks (group size G, 3B vs 7B model scale, classifier performance) strengthen the empirical picture.
weaknesses: Comparability of the headline SOTA claim is compromised: Stage 3 RL is trained on only a randomly sampled 10k subset of MIMIC-CXR (out of ~271k), while nearly all baselines are trained on the full training set. The 0.143 BLEU-4 result is therefore not obtained under the same data budget, and the claimed +5.1% improvement over AM-MRG is confounded. This is a substantive, not cosmetic, concern given the paper's central claim of new state-of-the-art benchmarks.
The choice to discard reports shorter than 30 tokens in the RL subset is only loosely justified and could bias the model toward longer, metric-friendlier reports, further inflating NLG comparisons.

Novelty is moderate. RER is a heuristic piecewise-linear scaling of the KL coefficient based on advantage and entropy, and VAPR (resetting reference and current policies to the best validation checkpoint) closely resembles standard checkpoint selection combined with periodic reference refresh; neither is analyzed theoretically, and the contribution reads primarily as an engineering combination.

VAPR's ablation may be confounded: resetting to the best validation checkpoint effectively performs strong model selection, so gains attributed to 'expanding the exploration space' cannot be cleanly separated from the benefit of retaining the best checkpoint (a form of early stopping available to any baseline).

The method optimizes a gameable proxy reward (BLEU-4 against the ground-truth reference) while simultaneously relaxing the KL constraint on high-advantage, high-reference-entropy responses — precisely the regime where the policy is most free to drift toward reference-copying behavior. This reward-hacking risk is acknowledged for EMA but not analyzed for the RER+VAPR combination; clinical fidelity could be improved via closer textual mimicry rather than genuine diagnostic accuracy.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs are reported; several headline gains are small in absolute terms (e.g., BLEU-4 0.136 to 0.143 on MIMIC-CXR, +0.007), so run-to-run variance matters.
The public code URL in the abstract is incomplete (dangling 'available at'), which weakens the reproducibility claim at submission time.

The mapping from normalized reference entropy to beta_i (Eq. 8-9) uses group-wise min-max normalization, which is degenerate when within-group entropy variance is small (a common case); no analysis of this failure mode is provided, and the beta bounds (0.05-0.12) look tightly tuned.

Test-time prompts include classifier-predicted disease labels, adding a dependency that propagates classifier errors; the classifier-agnostic claim is asserted but its sensitivity (e.g., with a weaker classifier) is not tested.
The paper lacks any limitations or societal-impact discussion, notable for a clinical application where errors in generated reports carry patient-safety implications.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated method: RER (response-level KL weighting based on advantage and reference entropy) and VAPR (periodic reset of reference/current policies to the validation-best checkpoint) are both simple, drop-in mechanisms, and the paper explains the intuitions well (Figs. 2, 3, Algorithm 1).

Comprehensive experimental evidence: results on both MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, ablations of every pipeline stage (Table 3) and each RL modification (Table 4), stability analyses (reward and KL curves in Fig. 3), group-size robustness (Sec. E), and model-size analysis (Sec. F).

Unusually thorough justification of design choices: the supplementary reward analysis (CheXpert F1 variance, RadGraph F1 reward inversion, BLEU-4/CheXpert advantage sign-consistency analysis) is a convincing empirical argument for the BLEU-4 reward, and the computational overhead of RER is honestly quantified (+1.9% step time, +3.9% memory).
Fair-comparison discussion (Table S9) explicitly catalogs the auxiliary supervision and evaluation-protocol changes used by competing methods, strengthening the credibility of the SOTA claims.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters for all three stages, prompt formats, classifier training details, and a stated public code release.
weaknesses: SOTA claims rest substantially on a confounded comparison: REVA-PO uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a much stronger recent LVLM backbone, while most baselines use older/smaller LLMs (GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, Llama-2-7B, Vicuna-13B). Absolute gains are small (e.g., BLEU-4 0.136→0.143 on MIMIC-CXR), so it is hard to disentangle the contribution of RER/VAPR from that of the stronger backbone. A GRPO baseline on the same backbone exists (Table 4), which helps, but the headline comparison would be more convincing with a same-backbone re-training of at least one strong baseline.

No statistical significance analysis or multi-seed results are reported; given the small absolute margins (0.003–0.007 BLEU-4) and the stochasticity of RL training, error bars or repeated runs would materially strengthen the claims.

VAPR repeatedly selects θ as the validation-best checkpoint (via a composite validation score with a tuned λ), which risks implicit overfitting to the validation set; the paper does not analyze sensitivity to λ or the reset period M.

Novelty is moderate: response-level β scaling and reference-policy resets are incremental combinations of known ideas (β-DPO, ε-DPO, Zheng et al.'s critic-based scaling, EMA/trust-region variants); the framing as Algorithms/General vs. an applied contribution could be clarified, and the theoretical grounding for the piecewise entropy-to-β mapping is heuristic.

RL Stage 3 is trained on only a 10k subsample of MIMIC-CXR with reports <30 tokens discarded; although val/test are untouched, the effect of this subsampling (and potential distribution shift toward longer reports) is not ablated.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract's code URL is truncated/empty; no human/radiologist evaluation despite the clinical setting; a few reference oddities (e.g., AM-MRG dated 2026, several arXiv-only citations).
